articles.title: Real Motors’ Project Ares is a cyberpunk fantasy made real
articles.body:
Electrification has done wonderful things for motorcycle design. By getting rid of the engine and the fuel tank that supports it, designers have the freedom to do whatever they want, and the results have been occasionally brilliant. I’m a big fan of the vaguely retrofuturistic stylings of the Maeving RM2 and the quirky minimalism of BMW’s CE 02, but nothing yet has quite left me so awestruck as Project Ares.
Real Motors’ Project Ares is a cyberpunk fantasy made real
Real Motors’ debut machine brings Night City vibes to the street, but it’s not the sportbike you might be expecting.
Real Motors’ Project Ares is a cyberpunk fantasy made real
Real Motors’ debut machine brings Night City vibes to the street, but it’s not the sportbike you might be expecting.
This all-electric machine is the first offering from South Carolina-based Real Motors, and it bears a shape that would not look out of place on the streets of Night City, the main setting in Cyberpunk 2077. There’s a little bit of Star Wars in there and maybe even some Wipeout, too, but it’s never derivative. Most importantly, it’s real. Project Ares starts at $20,000 and ships next year in limited volumes, but don’t let its future cafe racer vibe fool you. This doesn’t quite feel like you might expect.
Origins
CEO and cofounder Trent Dingman tells me that Real Motors started as a challenge between him and Michael Feng (design engineer and the other cofounder) to “build the coolest possible thing, the best design, and show people what we can do.”
Project Ares is the first coolest possible thing: an all-electric motorcycle designed and built in Greenville, right in the heart of the battery belt, not far from already-big and still-developing EV players like BMW, Scout Motors, Volvo, and Redwood Materials.
The white bike is an early prototype that’s substantially smaller than the bike I rode, Prototype 04, evocatively called “Ghost” thanks to its distinctive fairing. From a distance, it just looks like glossy black, nothing too special. Come closer, though, and you see the translucence. From in the saddle, you can spot the charger’s cooling vanes, situated inside where the tank would normally be. You can follow the bright orange high-voltage lines as they snake through and around the bike’s battery pack.
Things aren’t finalized yet, but that pack will be roughly 15 kilowatt-hours, charging at up to 3.3 kilowatts over a standard SAE J1772 charging port on the very top of its “tank.”
The pack powers an electric motor officially rated at 101 horsepower and an insane 738 pound-feet of torque. However, that latter figure requires some context. The number Real Motor quotes is the torque measured at the wheel, after being multiplied by the bike’s gearing. Most motorcycles quote actual torque at the engine or motor output shaft. Measured in the same way, the actual output of the Ares’ motor is probably somewhere closer to 200 pound-feet, still putting it among the strongest twisting motorcycles on the planet.
Those are substantial numbers, but then the Ares is carrying some substantial weight.
Ergonomics
While the Ares may look like it was sent from the future, it’s built in a present where we’re still stubbornly waiting for mass-produced solid-state batteries to fully enter reality. That means big batteries like this one weigh a lot.
Project Ares has a total weight of 485 pounds. That puts it right in line with Zero Motorcycles’ SR/F, which has similar power output and battery size. However, the Ares is nearly an inch and a half longer than the Zero.
From a more traditional sportbike perspective, the Ares weighs nearly 100 pounds more than a Ducati Panigale V4 and has a wheelbase roughly three-quarters of an inch longer.
Having only seen it in photos, I didn’t expect that volume. I had in my mind a diminutive cafe racer, the classic style of machine typified by British riders who like to splay themselves over their motorcycle’s tanks as they buzz from one cuppa to another.
And that’s definitely the way the Ares is set up. The bars are set low, putting your chest and head down close to that translucent tank. The pegs are likewise up high, delivering maximum clearance for cornering and putting you into that classic posture.
But whereas most cafe racers are skinny and svelte, the Ares has a wide saddle hinting at the mass of the machine beneath you. That aggressive geometry plus its weight made for a somewhat wobbly start as I got a feel for things, but I was quickly up to speed.
In the saddle
Riding “Ghost” was a refreshingly distraction-free experience. This prototype lacked mirrors, a choice prioritizing aesthetics over safety. But it did free me from worrying about anything behind. With only a minimalist LCD in front, I could focus exclusively on the ride.
Project Ares has three speed settings. Dingman warned me before I got in the saddle that the bike had neither traction control nor antilock braking. With that torque figure, theoretically enough to liquefy the rear tire, I started in mode 1, the lightest, to be safe.
I didn’t need to worry. While I’ve found some preproduction EVs to be a real handful, with overly aggressive throttles leading to bikes that want to buck you off the back, I immediately felt at home on the Ares. There’s no abrupt lurching forward as you twist the grip, just a smooth application of increasing power.
It wasn’t long before I was up to mode 2, then mode 3, then grinning like a fool with the throttle pegged wide open and my chest flat on the tank. Even in its most aggressive, the Ares is easy to manage, with plenty of power to entertain but such a smooth delivery that it never does anything unexpected.
What was unexpected was how it turns. Again, I had a vision of a razor-sharp racing machine, but the Ares takes a bit of muscle. Unlike the aforementioned Panigale, which drops onto its side with just a hint of pressure on the handlebars, the Ghost required a strong, sustained push to turn.
I wouldn’t call it reluctant as such, but the feeling is more of a cruiser than a sportbike. A cruiser with extremely sporty components, though. The unmarked suspension on my prototype felt plenty good, but buyers can spec top-shelf Öhlins dampers if they like. Brembo brakes are also on offer, meaning that while this bike comes at a premium price, you at least get premium components befitting something named after the son of Zeus.
Practicalities
So it’s a heavier, more intentional ride than its cafe racer style and ergos may imply, but the blame for much of that lies in today’s battery technology.
Which leads us to perhaps the biggest question of all: range. The Ares spec sheet lists 120 miles in the city on a charge. Frankly, I didn’t come close to that efficiency during my day in the saddle, but don’t hold that against it. It’s still pre-production, after all, and lots could change in the next few months.
Also, I spent a good portion of that day with the throttle pinned open, which is not ideal for maximizing longevity.
That said, I’ve yet to meet an electric motorcycle that can live up to its range estimates when ridden hard and at speed. I doubt this one will shatter that paradigm. Even so, Project Ares is already fast, fun, and astonishingly good looking. While the world of motorcycling may be evolving, style still counts for a lot.
Photography by Tim Stevens / The Verge

articles.title: Synaptics patent claims stop work on DisplayLink drivers
articles.body:
Synaptics patent claims stop work on DisplayLink drivers
[LWN subscriber-only content]
Mike Lothian owns a docking station (or dock) that uses a DisplayLink chipset that had, at least in his opinion, subpar performance on Linux. He decided to try improving the Linux driver, with LLM assistance, but ran into one problem that he could not solve—so he asked for help, hoping that Synaptics's developers would lend a hand. (DisplayLink was acquired by Synaptics in 2022.) Rather than help him in improving the driver, however, the Synaptics legal team responded with patent infringement claims, a demand that he cease unauthorized implementation of DisplayLink technology, and threats of expensive legal penalties. For now, it appears that Linux users of the company's docks will have to continue to live without feature parity with other platforms.
Synaptics and Displaylink
The dock that he was trying to support is a Dell device that connects to a system via USB 3 and allows users to connect multiple monitors and other devices to their computer. It provides its DisplayLink Manager (DLM) software for Linux for the devices via an APT repository for Ubuntu.
The company only provides DLM software in binary form, and only for x86-based platforms. The software is proprietary, but the company does maintain an open-source, out-of-tree kernel module that is included with DLM, the Extensible Virtual Display Interface (EVDI) project. It provides a driver that's compatible with Linux DRM and allows users to manage their docked displays with standard tools used for display settings, such as xrandr or GNOME and KDE Plasma's utilities.
A short article explains why the company has not released source code for DLM: the software uses a proprietary graphics technology called DL3 to create a compressed stream of the various channels (e.g., USB, DisplayLink video, audio) over a communication channel (USB 3 in this case) and decode it again for output to the user's devices.
Unfortunately, the vendor-supplied software did not work well for Lothian. I spoke and chatted with him via Signal while writing this article; he said that the driver kept crashing under Linux, so he decided to use his Claude subscription to try to develop a new driver and support software.
Vino
He posted the first
patch series for Vino—his Rust-based DRM/KMS driver—to the kernel's
dri-devel list as an RFC on June 17. Lothian noted that it was in an
incomplete state, and asked for help with a blocker that
he had run into trying to communicate with the dock's control plane. "
If you have
knowledge of the DisplayLink DL3 control-plane engagement sequence, or ideas for
isolating a whole-bus timing/ordering property a per-channel diff cannot see,
help would be very welcome.
" He received feedback from a few developers, including guidance
from Danilo Krummrich to rework the driver to use the Rust KMS bindings, but no advice
specific to the problem he was trying to solve.
Lothian also opened an issue on the EVDI GitHub repository on June 17. It explained the work he'd done so far, outlined the approach in trying to reverse-engineer the DL3 protocol, provided links to his GitHub repository with the Vino code, and asked for clarification on a few issues. There was no reply to his issue.
He also reached out to Łukasz Spintzyk of Synaptics directly by email; his correspondence with the company between July 5 and October 7 is available in this PDF compiled by Lothian. He noted that he had found a few bugs in EVDI and opened a pull request (that went unreviewed for several months), and also asked for assistance where he was blocked on Vino. On July 20, he received a reply, not from Spintzyk, but from Michal Lukaszek of Synaptics:
The reason I'm writing is that DisplayLink is not an open standard. The protocol, codec, and other technologies used by DisplayLink devices are proprietary to Synaptics and are protected by a substantial portfolio of patents in a number of jurisdictions, including the UK.
From what you've published, it appears that the VINO project is progressing beyond interoperability work and toward implementing technology that we believe is covered by those patents. While many developers understandably focus on avoiding copyrighted source code, patent law is different. An independently written or clean-room implementation does not necessarily avoid patent infringement if it implements patented inventions.
Lukaszek said it was entirely possible that Lothian was unaware of the
"
intellectual property landscape surrounding DisplayLink
", so he wanted
to make him aware now rather than "
have the situation become more formal
later
". Lothian lives in Scotland and has a ".co.uk" email address, which
explains why the email made reference to the UK.
Cease and desist
On August 17, Andrew Bateman, an assistant general council of
intellectual property for Synaptics, sent a cease-and-desist notice. The letter stated that Lothian had not
"
substantially responded
" to Lukaszek's communication, and had continued
with "
public statements and further development activities
". It included
an appendix with a list of 125 patents that "
cover fundamental aspects of
DisplayLink's architecture and operation
", but did not specify which patents
might be infringed by the work.
Synaptics included a list of eight demands it expected immediate compliance
with, including ceasing development of "
any software or other
implementation that infringes any Synaptics patent
", withdrawing submissions of
materials "
made to Linux kernel maintainers, mailing
lists, code-hosting platforms, package maintainers, distributions, or any other person or
organization
", and to identify in writing every location "
in which the
relevant materials have been published, submitted, stored, or
distributed
". It also demanded that he provide Synaptics with a signed
confirmation, by August 28, that he had complied with its demands.
Lothian, instead, posted version
three of his Vino work for the DisplayLink docks to the dri-devel list on
August 26. He said that the previous two versions had "
never lit a
panel
", but the new work could control three generations of DL3 docks
without any vendor software. There were no substantive reviews of the patch set
posted to the list, though there were some automated reviews from Sashiko.
On August 27, Lothian responded to Bateman and asked him to elaborate
on the patents that Synaptics thought were being infringed. "
A claim chart
mapping the relevant claims to the relevant code would make it much easier for
me to understand and properly respond to your concerns.
"
He also expressed confusion about Synaptics's position that his work was
being treated as patent infringement. Synaptics is a member of the Open Invention Network (OIN), which
was created to help open-source
developers and vendors deal with the threats of expensive patent litigation. It
holds a large, cross-licensed portfolio that serves to provide patent protection
to individuals, open-source projects, and large vendors alike. Lothian said that
he was now an OIN licensee as well, and he thought that it was supposed to
"
reduce exactly this sort of patent problem around Linux and open source
software
".
He asked Bateman to explain how Synaptics claims "
interact with our
respective OIN commitments
", and expressed a desire to sort things out with
Synaptics constructively. "
I don't think a public dispute between Synaptics
and an individual open source developer would be particularly helpful for either
of us, especially within the Linux and open source communities
".
Lothian did not think he could "
reasonably provide the signed undertaking
"
Synaptics had demanded by August 28 without understanding which patent
claims it was alleging. He asked for an extension to the deadline. There was no
response from Bateman, so Lothian sent a follow-up email on
September 18. He said he was concerned there was no acknowledgment to his 
last email, and wondered it was safe to assume he could continue his work. He
had been running the Vino driver himself for quite a while, and was eager to
move it upstream without having patent threats hanging over the work.
Bateman responded the next day and said that he should be concerned:
As you previously requested, we have been documenting your ongoing patent
infringement by mapping your Vino driver to specific claims of our DisplayLink
patents. I will provide this claim mapping documentation to you within the next
two weeks. I will also be sending to you our demand for substantial monetary
compensation to recoup the cost and effort required to create such documentation
of your infringing acts. I previously gave you the opportunity to stop your
infringement, but you decided to push back and not heed my warnings, and so now
we are escalating as we deem appropriate.
The letter continued to claim that Lothian would be "
single-handedly
eviscerating DisplayLink's competitive advantage in this crowded market by
educating our competitors and other third parties as to how we implement our
proprietary technology
". He said that DisplayLink is not a member of OIN,
and none of its technology is licensable through OIN or any other
organization.
Bateman sent a follow-up
letter, dated October 5, that included two claim charts for UK patents: GB2484736B ("Display control device") and GB2485613B ("Image generation"), both filed in 2010
and published in 2012. He reiterated Synaptics's demands from its previous
letter, and said that the deadline was now October 11; failure to comply
would result in the company seeking "
monetary
compensation from you in the amount of US$25,000 to recoup the costs and effort required to
create the attached documentation of your infringing acts
". That amount
would be increased by $25,000 each week until the company's demands were
complied with.
Lothian responded the next day, by email, to say that he was on
vacation, and would not be back home until October 13. He asked for an extension
of the deadline to return home and go through the claim charts "
ideally with
someone qualified to help me read them
". Bateman replied
that Synaptics would agree to extend the deadline to October 18, though no
further extensions would be granted. He reiterated that "
DisplayLink is not a
member of OIN
" and none of its technology was licensable through OIN.
OIN to the rescue?
Synaptics is a member of OIN, and is listed in the community directory. In addition to joining OIN, Lothian had reached out to the organization to try to solicit its help and has been in communication with some of the staff there. OIN indicated that it would look into the matter and see if he had any protection as an OIN member. That process took longer than Lothian hoped, though OIN did eventually provide its conclusion.
OIN's portfolio covers a wide range of software that matches its Linux System
Definition, but it does not cover everything that might be implemented for a
Linux system. In particular, its definition specifies that codecs ("
a
component of a program capable of performing transformations of a video, still
image or audio data stream or signal
") are not covered unless specifically
mentioned in this
list of components.
I spoke briefly to OIN CEO Keith Bergelt on October 23, shortly after OIN staff informed Lothian of the result of their research. Bergelt said that OIN's conclusion was that, since codecs are explicitly not covered by OIN's Linux System Definition, its protections did not extend to Lothian's attempted kernel contributions. OIN had recommended that Lothian reach out to a lawyer in the UK, and provided a recommendation.
Status
Unfortunately, that referral did not pan out, Lothian said. He has not given up
entirely, but he has taken down the GitHub repository to comply with Synaptics's
demands. For now, he may continue working on some of components that are not
affected by the patent claims, but the work on Vino will not be submitted
to the kernel. "
Vino itself has to remain local until this is sorted out, I
just can't afford to defend myself against Synaptics.
"
Perhaps amusingly, Lothian told me that someone from Synaptics finally
replied to the pull request on October 7. Lothian told me he does not
intend to follow up on the comments: "
You can't threaten to sue me and then
say 'can you update your pull request?'
"
For the time being, Synaptics has succeeded in shutting down an effort to improve the way DisplayLink docks work with Linux. It is an unpleasant reminder that, while much of the current conversations in open-source communities are concerned with LLM-driven development, software patents still pose problems for free-software developers and users.

He noted that he had found a few bugs in EVDI and opened a pull request (that went unreviewed for several months), and also asked for assistance where he was blocked on Vino. On July 20, he received a reply, not from Spintzyk, but from Michal Lukaszek of Synaptics:
The reason I'm writing is that DisplayLink is not an open standard. The protocol, codec, and other technologies used by DisplayLink devices are proprietary to Synaptics and are protected by a substantial portfolio of patents in a number of jurisdictions, including the UK.
From what you've published, it appears that the VINO project is progressing beyond interoperability work and toward implementing technology that we believe is covered by those patents. While many developers understandably focus on avoiding copyrighted source code, patent law is different. An independently written or clean-room implementation does not necessarily avoid patent infringement if it implements patented inventions.
Lukaszek said it was entirely possible that Lothian was unaware of the
"
intellectual property landscape surrounding DisplayLink
", so he wanted
to make him aware now rather than "
have the situation become more formal
later
". Lothian lives in Scotland and has a ".co.uk" email address, which
explains why the email made reference to the UK.
Cease and desist
On August 17, Andrew Bateman, an assistant general council of
intellectual property for Synaptics, sent a cease-and-desist notice. The letter stated that Lothian had not
"
substantially responded
" to Lukaszek's communication, and had continued
with "
public statements and further development activities
". It included
an appendix with a list of 125 patents that "
cover fundamental aspects of
DisplayLink's architecture and operation
", but did not specify which patents
might be infringed by the work.
Synaptics included a list of eight demands it expected immediate compliance
with, including ceasing development of "
any software or other
implementation that infringes any Synaptics patent
", withdrawing submissions of
materials "
made to Linux kernel maintainers, mailing
lists, code-hosting platforms, package maintainers, distributions, or any other person or
organization
", and to identify in writing every location "
in which the
relevant materials have been published, submitted, stored, or
distributed
". It also demanded that he provide Synaptics with a signed
confirmation, by August 28, that he had complied with its demands.
Lothian, instead, posted version
three of his Vino work for the DisplayLink docks to the dri-devel list on
August 26. He said that the previous two versions had "
never lit a
panel
", but the new work could control three generations of DL3 docks
without any vendor software. There were no substantive reviews of the patch set
posted to the list, though there were some automated reviews from Sashiko.
On August 27, Lothian responded to Bateman and asked him to elaborate
on the patents that Synaptics thought were being infringed. "
A claim chart
mapping the relevant claims to the relevant code would make it much easier for
me to understand and properly respond to your concerns.
"
He also expressed confusion about Synaptics's position that his work was
being treated as patent infringement. Synaptics is a member of the Open Invention Network (OIN), which
was created to help open-source
developers and vendors deal with the threats of expensive patent litigation. It
holds a large, cross-licensed portfolio that serves to provide patent protection
to individuals, open-source projects, and large vendors alike. Lothian said that
he was now an OIN licensee as well, and he thought that it was supposed to
"
reduce exactly this sort of patent problem around Linux and open source
software
".
He asked Bateman to explain how Synaptics claims "
interact with our
respective OIN commitments
", and expressed a desire to sort things out with
Synaptics constructively. "
I don't think a public dispute between Synaptics
and an individual open source developer would be particularly helpful for either
of us, especially within the Linux and open source communities
".
Lothian did not think he could "
reasonably provide the signed undertaking
"
Synaptics had demanded by August 28 without understanding which patent
claims it was alleging. He asked for an extension to the deadline. There was no
response from Bateman, so Lothian sent a follow-up email on
September 18. He said he was concerned there was no acknowledgment to his 
last email, and wondered it was safe to assume he could continue his work. He
had been running the Vino driver himself for quite a while, and was eager to
move it upstream without having patent threats hanging over the work.
Bateman responded the next day and said that he should be concerned:
As you previously requested, we have been documenting your ongoing patent
infringement by mapping your Vino driver to specific claims of our DisplayLink
patents. I will provide this claim mapping documentation to you within the next
two weeks. I will also be sending to you our demand for substantial monetary
compensation to recoup the cost and effort required to create such documentation
of your infringing acts. I previously gave you the opportunity to stop your
infringement, but you decided to push back and not heed my warnings, and so now
we are escalating as we deem appropriate.
The letter continued to claim that Lothian would be "
single-handedly
eviscerating DisplayLink's competitive advantage in this crowded market by
educating our competitors and other third parties as to how we implement our
proprietary technology
". He said that DisplayLink is not a member of OIN,
and none of its technology is licensable through OIN or any other
organization.
Bateman sent a follow-up
letter, dated October 5, that included two claim charts for UK patents: GB2484736B ("Display control device") and GB2485613B ("Image generation"), both filed in 2010
and published in 2012. He reiterated Synaptics's demands from its previous
letter, and said that the deadline was now October 11; failure to comply
would result in the company seeking "
monetary
compensation from you in the amount of US$25,000 to recoup the costs and effort required to
create the attached documentation of your infringing acts
". That amount
would be increased by $25,000 each week until the company's demands were
complied with.
Lothian responded the next day, by email, to say that he was on
vacation, and would not be back home until October 13. He asked for an extension
of the deadline to return home and go through the claim charts "
ideally with
someone qualified to help me read them
". Bateman replied
that Synaptics would agree to extend the deadline to October 18, though no
further extensions would be granted. He reiterated that "
DisplayLink is not a
member of OIN
" and none of its technology was licensable through OIN.
OIN to the rescue?
Synaptics is a member of OIN, and is listed in the community directory. In addition to joining OIN, Lothian had reached out to the organization to try to solicit its help and has been in communication with some of the staff there. OIN indicated that it would look into the matter and see if he had any protection as an OIN member. That process took longer than Lothian hoped, though OIN did eventually provide its conclusion.
OIN's portfolio covers a wide range of software that matches its Linux System
Definition, but it does not cover everything that might be implemented for a
Linux system. In particular, its definition specifies that codecs ("
a
component of a program capable of performing transformations of a video, still
image or audio data stream or signal
") are not covered unless specifically
mentioned in this
list of components.
I spoke briefly to OIN CEO Keith Bergelt on October 23, shortly after OIN staff informed Lothian of the result of their research. Bergelt said that OIN's conclusion was that, since codecs are explicitly not covered by OIN's Linux System Definition, its protections did not extend to Lothian's attempted kernel contributions. OIN had recommended that Lothian reach out to a lawyer in the UK, and provided a recommendation.
Status
Unfortunately, that referral did not pan out, Lothian said. He has not given up
entirely, but he has taken down the GitHub repository to comply with Synaptics's
demands. For now, he may continue working on some of components that are not
affected by the patent claims, but the work on Vino will not be submitted
to the kernel. "
Vino itself has to remain local until this is sorted out, I
just can't afford to defend myself against Synaptics.
"
Perhaps amusingly, Lothian told me that someone from Synaptics finally
replied to the pull request on October 7. Lothian told me he does not
intend to follow up on the comments: "
You can't threaten to sue me and then
say 'can you update your pull request?'
"
For the time being, Synaptics has succeeded in shutting down an effort to improve the way DisplayLink docks work with Linux. It is an unpleasant reminder that, while much of the current conversations in open-source communities are concerned with LLM-driven development, software patents still pose problems for free-software developers and users.

articles.title: AMD's Zen 6 Family: Feeding the Beast
articles.body:
Hello you fine Internet folks,
Today we’re looking at AMD’s next-generation Zen 6 CPU core family. We’ll explore the changes from Zen 5 and what the differences between Zen 6 and Zen 6c tell us about AMD’s approach to microarchitecture.
Hope y’all enjoy!
Overview
From a bird's eye view, Zen 6 is the natural evolution of Zen5, with the expansion of many OoO structures and iterative improvements found throughout the core.
Digging in deeper however tells a different story, with AMD heavily re-working several parts of the core, reminding me of the changes from Zen 1 to Zen 2.
At a high level the changes AMD made to the integer schedules stand out, returning to a layout reminiscent of Zen 3 and Zen 4.
Branch Prediction
Zen 5 had the best direction predictor of any core we have measured and Zen 6 seemingly builds upon that same direction predictor.
The biggest difference we do see is in what happens once the direction predictor gets overwhelmed. Both cores hit that wall in about the same place and past it, the predictor is left guessing at random data, so the time per branch mostly reflects how long the core takes to recover from a wrong guess. 
That plateau sits at roughly 3.5 to 4 ns of extra time per branch on Zen 5 and roughly 3 to 3.5 ns on Zen 6 so Zen 6 is paying less for each branch it gets wrong, which speaks to AMD reducing the latency of a branch mispredict compared to Zen 5.
Zen 6 has also improved the ability of the core to do 2 branches per cycle with Zen 6 able to do 2 branches per cycle within the L1 instruction cache.
When the footprint exceeds the L1i, then it falls to just a single branch per cycle for the rest of the BTB except for the 64B test which goes up to 4 cycles per branch for the L2 BTB.
When comparing the BTB of Zen 6 to Zen 5, Zen 6 appears to have focused on improving the speed of the BTB compared to beefing up the capacity.
The accuracy of Zen 6’s Branch Predictor Unit is very similar to Zen 5’s while also being faster which is a good thing considering that Zen 5 already had a very accurate Branch Predictor.
Instruction Fetch
Zen 6 carries forward the same dual decode cluster schema that Zen 5 introduced but, unlike Zen 5 where a single thread could only effectively use a single decode cluster, now with Zen 6 a single thread can use both decode clusters.
Outside of the L1i, Zen 6 looks very similar to Zen 5’s behavior on the instruction side of things.
Execution Engine
The execution engine of Zen 6 is overall very similar to Zen 5, but there are some important differences to be mindful of.
On the integer side, Zen 6 brings back Zen 4’s NOP pairing behavior, retiring up to 16 NOPs per cycle. Zen 6 also comes closer to theoretical peak throughput for simple integer instructions than Zen 5, sustaining 5.96 64-bit adds per cycle against Zen 5’s 5.25 with the same six ALUs.
AMD has reduced the number of integer multiply units from three to two, with PDEP and PEXT throughput also falling from three instructions per cycle to two. According to AMD, Zen 5’s third integer multiply unit did not justify its area cost.
On the vector side, the floating-point units are unchanged, with Zen 6 still handling two 512-bit FADDs, FMULs, or FMAs per cycle. The change is in VNNI, where Zen 6 doubles the number of units from two to four and our 512-bit VNNI test goes from 1.99 to 3.88 instructions per cycle, with Zen 6c matching it. VNNI instructions are useful for operations like calculating the inner loop of quantized inference as well as for video codecs using them for video filters as well.
Moving over to the other notable change, Zen 5 could already perform four per cycle, but our test shows only two of them could be vector loads, regardless of if they were 256 or 512 bit loads. Zen 6 raises 256-bit loads to four per cycle on both cores while leaving 512-bit loads at two, so both widths now reach the same 128 bytes per cycle which matters because most shipped vector code still targets AVX1/2.
The Out of Order Engine: Where Zen 6 and Zen 6c Split
In the past the difference between the Classic cores and the Dense cores in terms of the architecture were, for all intents and purposes, functionally identical with the biggest changes being in the number of cores on a CCD and the amount of L3 cache per core. With the Zen 6 family, that has changed.
Starting inside of the core, the changes occur after micro-op dispatch and seemingly end after the load queue.
The main differences between Zen 6 and Zen 6c lie in the capacities of their out-of-order structures. Several of these structures are larger on Zen 6c, allowing it to keep more work in flight and absorb more latency than Zen 6. The reorder buffer grows from 576 to 640 entries, the integer register file from 288 to 352, the vector scheduler from 138 to 180, and the load queue from 280 to 330.
The differences suggest that AMD is specializing the two designs. Zen 6 appears tuned for high frequency, while Zen 6c has more capacity to tolerate comparatively high memory latency.
Zen 6 and Zen 6c use 12-core and 32-core CCDs, respectively, but both provide 4 MB of L3 cache per core. That gives the 12-core CCD 48 MB of L3 cache and the 32-core CCD 128 MB.
L3 latency has increased from about 47 cycles on Zen 5 to 55 cycles on Zen 6 and 66 cycles on Zen 6c. The larger caches and greater number of mesh stops likely contribute to the increase. In nanoseconds, Zen 6’s higher clock hides most of the increase, at 10.7 ns against 10.3 ns on the Zen 5-based EPYC 9355P, while Zen 6c’s lower clock and larger CCX put it at 16.4 ns.
Moving over to bandwidth, we see that Zen 6 fixes Zen 5’s odd L2 bandwidth behavior, where a core pulled only about 42 bytes per cycle across most of the L2’s capacity, in Zen 6 the read path now reliably delivers 64 bytes per cycle. The rest of the cache hierarchy is largely unchanged in bandwidth per cycle.
Load/Store
Store-to-load forwarding is seemingly unchanged from Zen 5 and is where the behavior of Zen 6 and Zen 6c re-unify.
A 32-bit load from the same address as a 64-bit store completes with effectively zero latency which lets Zen 6 handle two dependent store-load pairs per cycle. Loads fully contained within the store complete in 7 cycles regardless of alignment with partial overlaps costing 14 cycles, matching Zen 5.
SPEC CPU 2026 Performance
The EPYC 9686F is near the top of our estimated single-threaded SPEC CPU 2026 results. It roughly matches the Ryzen 9 9950X3D2, AMD’s highest-end client CPU from the previous generation, in integer rate and beats it in floating-point rate. At a matched 4.1 GHz, the 9686F leads the 9950X3D2 by about 4% in integer and 11% in floating point, despite the X3D part’s much larger L3.
The EPYC 9996 is no slouch either. It roughly matches the previous-generation EPYC 9575F in single-threaded performance, despite running at lower clocks and having four times as many cores. It also edges out NVIDIA’s Vera in integer and leads it by about 20% in floating point.
The EPYC 9686F leads on almost every subtest and finishes about 18% ahead of the EPYC 9996 in both suites. It scores 6.20 versus 5.25 in integer and 10.6 versus 8.99 in floating point, with some of its largest leads in 714.cpython, 766.femflow, and 772.marian.
Against the Zen 5-based EPYC 9575F, the 9996 scores 5.25 versus 5.13 in integer and 8.99 versus 9.01 in floating point while running about 900 MHz slower. The 9996 also edges out the 9686F in 721.gcc and 765.roms, two subtests where the 9686F’s higher clock provides no advantage.
Top-down breakdowns of pipeline slots on the two Zen 6 chips show where the 9686F’s lead comes from. The integer-rate profiles look almost identical in core-bound subtests. In 750.sealcrypto, 710.omnetpp, 735.gem5, and 753.ns3, retiring slots account for nearly the same share on both chips, with differences of less than one percentage point.
Memory-heavy subtests show larger gaps. Moving from the EPYC 9996 to the EPYC 9686F, backend memory stalls rise from 37.9% to 50.0% of pipeline slots in 729.abc, from 19.0% to 34.1% in 723.llvm, and from 24.8% to 33.2% in 708.sqlite. The share of retiring slots falls accordingly. Zen 6c’s lower clock and larger shared L3 cache may help explain its lower memory-stall share.
The floating-point profiles look similar for most subtests. The retiring share in 731.astcenc, 772.marian, and 767.nest differs by about one percentage point or less, and 709.cactus spends over half its slots stalled on front-end bandwidth on both chips.
The larger gaps again appear in memory-heavy subtests. Moving from the EPYC 9996 to the EPYC 9686F, backend memory stalls rise from 42.5% to 55.3% of slots in 765.roms, from 60.9% to 67.6% in 749.fotonik3d, and from 17.8% to 33.8% in 782.lbm. These are also tests where the 9686F’s higher clock helps least: it trails the 9996 in 765.roms, roughly ties in 749.fotonik3d, and leads by about 11% in 782.lbm, despite clocking up to roughly 29% higher.
Running the 9686F at 4.1 GHz to match the 9996 removes the clock advantage, and the overall picture flips: the 9686F scores 4.92 and 8.64 at that clock, putting Zen 6c about 6.7% ahead per clock in integer and 4% in floating point. At the same clock speed, Zen 6 and Zen 6c look almost identical in core-bound integer subtests. In 750.sealcrypto, retiring slots account for 67.3% of the total on the EPYC 9686F versus 67.6% on the EPYC 9996.The floating-point profiles also look similar in several subtests at matched clocks. Both chips spend over half their pipeline slots stalled on frontend bandwidth in 709.cactus. Their retiring shares differ by about two percentage points in 722.palm and 766.femflow.
The 9686F still spends a larger share of its pipeline slots stalled on memory. Backend memory stalls account for 50.3% versus 42.5% on the 9996 in 765.roms, 24.9% versus 17.8% in 782.lbm, and 63.3% versus 60.9% in 749.fotonik3d. Zen 6c’s 128 MB L3 cache is likely serving more of these requests than Zen 6’s 48 MB cache, reducing the need to access main memory.
The clearest difference is in frontend latency stalls, which account for a much larger share of slots on the 9686F in subtests with large codebases. In 727.cppcheck, that share is 35.2% versus 16.6% on the 9996; in 721.gcc, it is 25.8% versus 10.0%. With clock speed matched and both designs sharing the same frontend, those stalls most likely reflect differences in the cache and memory hierarchy.
The floating-point profiles also look similar in several subtests at matched clocks. Both chips spend over half their pipeline slots stalled on frontend bandwidth in 709.cactus. Their retiring shares differ by about two percentage points in 722.palm and 766.femflow.
The 9686F still spends a larger share of its pipeline slots stalled on memory. Backend memory stalls account for 50.3% versus 42.5% on the 9996 in 765.roms, 24.9% versus 17.8% in 782.lbm, and 63.3% versus 60.9% in 749.fotonik3d. Zen 6c’s 128 MB L3 cache is likely serving more of these requests than Zen 6’s 48 MB cache, reducing the need to access main memory.
Final Words
The Zen 6 Family improves upon its predecessor in various ways, an upgraded frontend allows one thread to utilize both decoders, while a faster branch predictor makes it more forgiving on misses, all tied together with larger OoO structures allowing it to better hide memory stalls. All of this coming together to provide a generational uplift from Zen 5.
However, I think the more interesting change is the split between Zen 6 and Zen 6c. The classic and dense cores now differ within the out-of-order engine, with Zen 6 appearing tuned for higher clocks and Zen 6c providing more capacity to absorb latency. The shared foundation is still clear, but those differences make the choice between them more dependent on workload behavior.
The performance results are encouraging as well with the estimated single-threaded SPEC CPU 2026 scores, the EPYC 9686F leads the Zen 5-based EPYC 9575F by about 21% in integer and 18% in floating point. The EPYC 9996 roughly matches the 9575F despite running about 900 MHz slower which are strong results for both core designs.
AMD’s answer to the classic-versus-dense question used to be the same core at two densities but now with Zen 6 it is two cores, each shaped for where it will run. That now leaves me wondering what AMD will do with the Zen 7 Family and if we will see even more specialization of the same basic core design or if we will see a larger split of the designs.

Zen 6c’s 128 MB L3 cache is likely serving more of these requests than Zen 6’s 48 MB cache, reducing the need to access main memory.
The clearest difference is in frontend latency stalls, which account for a much larger share of slots on the 9686F in subtests with large codebases. In 727.cppcheck, that share is 35.2% versus 16.6% on the 9996; in 721.gcc, it is 25.8% versus 10.0%. With clock speed matched and both designs sharing the same frontend, those stalls most likely reflect differences in the cache and memory hierarchy.
The floating-point profiles also look similar in several subtests at matched clocks. Both chips spend over half their pipeline slots stalled on frontend bandwidth in 709.cactus. Their retiring shares differ by about two percentage points in 722.palm and 766.femflow.
The 9686F still spends a larger share of its pipeline slots stalled on memory. Backend memory stalls account for 50.3% versus 42.5% on the 9996 in 765.roms, 24.9% versus 17.8% in 782.lbm, and 63.3% versus 60.9% in 749.fotonik3d. Zen 6c’s 128 MB L3 cache is likely serving more of these requests than Zen 6’s 48 MB cache, reducing the need to access main memory.
Final Words
The Zen 6 Family improves upon its predecessor in various ways, an upgraded frontend allows one thread to utilize both decoders, while a faster branch predictor makes it more forgiving on misses, all tied together with larger OoO structures allowing it to better hide memory stalls. All of this coming together to provide a generational uplift from Zen 5.
However, I think the more interesting change is the split between Zen 6 and Zen 6c. The classic and dense cores now differ within the out-of-order engine, with Zen 6 appearing tuned for higher clocks and Zen 6c providing more capacity to absorb latency. The shared foundation is still clear, but those differences make the choice between them more dependent on workload behavior.
The performance results are encouraging as well with the estimated single-threaded SPEC CPU 2026 scores, the EPYC 9686F leads the Zen 5-based EPYC 9575F by about 21% in integer and 18% in floating point. The EPYC 9996 roughly matches the 9575F despite running about 900 MHz slower which are strong results for both core designs.
AMD’s answer to the classic-versus-dense question used to be the same core at two densities but now with Zen 6 it is two cores, each shaped for where it will run. That now leaves me wondering what AMD will do with the Zen 7 Family and if we will see even more specialization of the same basic core design or if we will see a larger split of the designs.

articles.title: Blender 5.3 released with Gaussian Splat support
articles.body:
Watch the Recap Video
Make a Splat
Gaussian Magic
Point of View
Radiant Future
More About Shading
CYCLES
Divide and Shine
CYCLES
A diamond
in the Rough
CYCLES
Gone with Denoise
NVIDIA DLSS brings near-final render quality to the viewport, making lighting and look development faster and more responsive while virtually eliminating flickering between frames during animation playback.
Find it in the Denoise panel under Render properties, Sampling.
DLSS denoising requires NVIDIA driver version 620 or newer.
EEVEE
Lights Meet Material Nodes
Lighting to Your Liking
A Wider Perspective
EEVEE can now render panoramic cameras, supporting all types of projections, from equirectangular and cubemap formats to various fisheye models and mirror ball.
The current implementation has a few limitations: depth of field, raytracing, and volumetric temporal reprojection in the viewport are not yet supported.
More in EEVEE & Viewport
COMPOSITOR
Side Effects
You can now stack Effects on your scene just like you would modifiers or constraints.
Applying compositing effects has never been easier.
One-click, Bloom!
Choose from built-in effects such as Bloom, Chromatic Aberration, Film Grain, and Vignette, as well as effects from online asset libraries or your own custom compositor node groups.
Internally, each effect is its own node group, with its output passed on to the next effect.
You can further customize effects at any time in the Compositor editor.
COMPOSITOR
Bundle Up
17 Geometry Nodes are now supported in the Compositor, bringing a range of new capabilities across bundles, math and logic, and utility operations.
This includes bundle support with Get Bundle Item, Store Bundle Item, Combine Bundle, Typed Bundle, and Separate Bundle.
Math and logic nodes such as Boolean Math, Compare, Float to Integer, Integer Math, Matrix SVD, Combine Transform, and Separate Transform. Plus utility nodes including Hash Value, Random Value, Is Viewport, Import Text, and Bone Info.
Play Fast
Playback is now up to 2x faster on GPU, particularly when playing back EXR sequences.
The interactive compositor now supports playback caching. It can be enabled from the sidebar, Options panel.
Anisotropic Kuwahara is now up to 10x faster on Apple GPUs, 2x faster on NVIDIA GPUs, and 25-30% on CPU.
More in Compositor
Study the artwork
Blender splash artwork source files are available for you to play with!
CORE
Blender, meet projects.
Until now, Blender’s preferences (such as asset libraries) were shared across all projects, and it was up to users to keep related files and resources organized.
Blender now supports projects, giving you a way to group related files, share resources, and manage settings across an entire project, whether you’re working alone or as part of a team.
Everything
Everywhere
All In a Project
Projects support custom variables that can be used throughout a project, such as a character’s name or a frequently used file path.
Per-project asset libraries and color management configurations are also supported. You can even set up a custom splash screen for your project, providing quick access to its files and other recent projects.
Add-ons and other extensions per-project will follow in future Blender versions.
Projects are entirely optional, most of the time you’ll probably work without one.
ASSETS
Asset Libraries ♥ Extensions
Asset libraries can now be shared as extensions! Just like add-ons or themes.
Browse hundreds of public domain assets available on the Extensions platform via the Get Extensions tab and install them directly from within Blender.
GREASE PENCIL
Drawn to Select
Draw Mode now has its own selection tools: Tweak, Lasso, Box, and Circle. Select strokes and adjust them right where you draw.
Move, rotate, scale, duplicate, copy, paste, and delete strokes using the usual shortcuts, or access all these actions from the new Stroke menu.
Carve Diem
Meet the new Carver tool in Draw Mode.
It cuts shapes using proper Boolean subtraction, creating clean cuts in strokes and fills based on a lasso selection. Holes are created automatically when needed.
When a shape has both a stroke and a fill, carving a hole into it also creates a stroke around the hole. Fills that are split apart become separate shapes, making them easy to sculpt further.
One Tool to Fill Them All
The Fill tool can now fill multiple regions at once.
Simply draw a path across multiple regions to fill them all as a single shape, with no gaps or borders in between.
Ramp It Up
Gradient fills now use a ColorRamp input instead of being limited to just two colors.
Flip Out
Mirror the camera view horizontally with the new Flip View operator to evaluate the composition from a different perspective and spot asymmetry or visual imbalances.
This only affects the viewport display. It does not change the camera object’s transform or the final render, which remains unchanged. Use the operator again to restore the original orientation.
Flip View has no shortcut assigned by default, but you can assign your own through the right-click menu or add it to Quick Favorites (Q) for easy access.
I/O
USD Collection Importer
Collections can now be associated to importers.
Similar to the Collection Exporters introduced in Blender 4.2 LTS, Collection Importers make it easy to re-import data with a single click, without having to navigate menus or adjust settings repeatedly.
Configure them through the Importers panel under Collection Properties. Settings are stored in .blend files, making them easy to share and preserving them across Blender sessions.
Only the USD importer is supported in Blender 5.3.
See all USD, Alembic, glTF, OpenEXR, and other I/O changes.
VIDEO SEQUENCER
Cut to the chase
The Video Sequencer gets a full ripple editing framework, a rewritten blade tool, and a long list of editing, interface, and performance improvements, including initial OpenTimelineIO support.
Ripple,
Shuffle,
Overwrite
Welcome Ripple editing to Blender 5.3!
This new overlap mode automatically moves strips forward or backward as edits are made, maintaining timeline continuity without the need to manually close gaps.
Ripple, Shuffle, and Overwrite modes are now consistently used across editing operations. Switch between them while moving strips using R, S, and V.
Making Waves
Complete the ripple workflow with these handy operators:
Ripple Add: Hold Shift while dragging and dropping strips to insert them using ripple behavior, automatically making room in the timeline.
Ripple Trim: Trim selected strips at the playhead and automatically close the resulting gaps. Use Shift+Q or Shift+W to trim from either side.
Ripple Delete: Delete selected strips and move subsequent content back to close the gaps. Use Shift+X.
Cutting Edge: Blade 2.0
Splits are now visualized as a line when using Blade and as a region when using Box Blade. Tooltips display frame values at the split location, while a real-time preview shows the frame beneath the cursor.
Press and hold C in the timeline to temporarily activate the Blade tool.
Release it to switch back to the previously active tool.
But wait, there’s more: Hardware decoding, thumbnail support for Scene and other strips, OpenTimelineIO import and export, and much more.
USER INTERFACE
Search. Sort. Scribble.
Sorted Out
Arrange your objects freely with custom sorting in the Outliner. Finally.
Switch back to alphabetical order from the header popover.
Plus improvements to filtering, drag-and-drop behavior, and hierarchy management.
Side Quest
Sidebars in all editors now support search, making it possible to find any property or operator, even inside tabs created by add-ons.
Press Ctrl/Cmd + F while hovering the sidebar and start typing right away, or through the context menu of the tabs and panels.
To clear the search, press Alt/Option + F.
Mark it Down
The Blender UI now supports rendering basic Markdown formatting.
In node editors, write markdown directly in the new Comment node, or in regular layouts for scripts/add-ons through the label_markdown widget. Another handy widget for long strings is label_multiline, it behaves just like labels but allows text to wrap.
But wait: IME support, improved tooltips, box-select gesture, browsable node editor context paths, better Attribute Viewer overlay, Curve widget selection, and more!
What’s Next?
Blender on tablets, texture layers, animation layers? Show your support for upcoming development projects and help shape the future of Blender.
BUT WAIT, THERE’S MORE
Plus hundreds of bug fixes, code cleanups and refactors.
See the full list of changes.
CREDITS
Blender is a community project.
Learn more on how you can contribute to Blender.
List of developers who contributed to Blender 5.3 and all-time contributors.
Splash artwork: OVERGROWN, by Blender Studio
Cycles diamonds render by Chris Tyler. Butterflies specter shader by Cartesian Caramel. Grease Pencil drawings by Vivien Lulkowski from Blender Studio, Cowboi and Storm by Blender Studio.
Huge thanks to everyone involved! 🧡
The Blender team. November 10, 2026

articles.title: Meet the Sad Wives of AI
articles.body:
If i had to listen to another minute of my husband talking about Claude Code, I might have actually died. It was 11 pm in Berkeley, California, where I was home alone with our 10-month-old daughter, and 2 am in Cambridge, Massachusetts, where he was visiting for his newish job in AI. “JUST LOOK AT THIS!” he shouted. The FaceTime camera zoomed toward a laptop sitting on a hotel bed. “SEE?!”
See what, I thought. I wanted to shower. I still had to take the dog out.
“ARE YOU LOOKING?” he shouted again. I wasn’t. I was looking at our real baby. But that’s the thing. There are two babies in this household now: the small human one and the large language model. Both demand constant attention. Both keep us up at 2 am.
Is this a Sophie’s choice kind of situation? Please. I’d kill the AI baby in an instant.
There’s a strange and under-discussed side effect of the AI boom: what it’s doing to family dynamics. By which I mean: how it’s potentially destroying family dynamics. I’m sure this applies to all kinds of families, gay or straight, rich or poor, with any AI-pilled members. The technology is coming, has come, for us all. But for the purposes of this story, I mostly spoke to white-collar heteros in the Bay Area, because that’s where a certain psychological crisis seems most acute. Often it goes like this: He works in AI, and she does everything and anything else. Other times, it’s bleaker: He desperately wants to work in AI—or feels he must work in AI—and she wants him to do literally anything else.
Either way, the men go in and the women want out. How many? It depends on how you define “working in AI.” About 71 percent of “AI-skilled workers,” according to one report, are men, and there are roughly 35,000 open AI roles in the US at any given moment. Broaden that to include investors and you’re adding thousands more. Broaden it further to include every man who has mentioned to his wife that he is “looking at some opportunities in the space”—and we’re in the millions. Conservatively, that means hundreds of thousands of spouses, partners, and girlfriends, holding down the fort while someone mansplains the singularity to them. There are, in other words, a lot of us, and more of us are surfacing—gasping for air and a single conversation that doesn’t involve LLMs—by the day.
There’s a name for our ranks. I call us the sad wives of AI.
First of all, I’m sorry. AI is already the only thing most people talk about here, and it’s even worse for the sad wives.
One of them moved from New York for her husband’s career. He cofounded an AI company; now he’s head of design at another. “He’s so passionate about it,” she says. “I go along to get along.” That is, when she can remember what it is he does, exactly. “My eyes glaze over a bit. I tend to check out. I forget.” She does say his company is at the forefront of … something. Mostly, she’s tired. “I did not expect how homogenous it would be,” she says. “In New York, I had a friend who’s a teacher, a friend who’s a nurse, a friend in fashion, a friend in finance—and none of us talked about our jobs when we went out. Every time I go out in San Francisco, it feels like I’m at a work happy hour. I don’t get it.”
In a way, it can’t be helped. Most days it feels like every billboard in the city is about AI. Every. Single. One. “I’m on the edge,” another AI wife tells me, “while my husband drives by and is like, ‘Oh wow, that’s my company’s billboard.’ Cool. Great.” She, like almost every sad AI wife I talk to, doesn’t want me to include the specifics of her situation. Marriages, social standings, and finances—anything to protect the equity!—are on the line.
Some of the sad wives are obscenely rich; others are struggling. But the more I talk to them, the more I hear the same lines, the same complaints, the same clichés. The hours. The obsession. The sense that missing this moment would mean, for their AI-pilled spouses, missing the most important technological shift of a lifetime. “They really want to ride the wave,” one AI wife says. Another: “He’s always depressed about something.”
Yana van der Meulen Rodgers, the chair of labor studies and employment relations at Rutgers University, has a blunt take: What’s happening in Bay Area households isn’t just a lifestyle story. It’s a labor market story. The AI boom, Rodgers says, is creating a “perfect storm” of forces reshaping household dynamics, playing out along predictably gendered lines.
The story is older than Silicon Valley, of course. Every major technological boom has produced the same figure, the person who gives everything to the wave. During the industrial revolution, it was the factory worker. During the Gold Rush, it was the men who left their families and headed west. During the dotcom boom, it was the founders sleeping under their desks in SoMa. Now, it is the person who is building, building, always building—vibe coding at midnight, constantly upgrading their models—convinced that stopping for five minutes means missing everything. Economists call this the “ideal worker.” Rodgers calls it a trap. “Someone who works many hours, giving all of themselves to this new force,” she says. “That means less time at home for the partner, less time for care work.”
Though things keep changing, some analyses suggest that women are about 20 percent less likely than men to use generative AI. “It’s a function not of gender per se,” Rodgers suggests, “but of the occupations that women hold.” Women are disproportionately represented in jobs—education, health care, social services—that right now use AI less. The result could be a compounding disadvantage. Over time, it means less access to the boom’s financial rewards, more responsibility for the domestic labor it generates.
And what happens when it doesn’t work out for the men? Many, if not most, won’t make it in AI, a lucrative but volatile business. “With job loss comes some depression,” Rodgers says. “Within the household, if one person is going through adverse mental health effects around job loss or uncertainty, the other naturally becomes the support person.” The cruel irony, for some sad wives, is that the moment their husband does leave AI, whether by choice or by force, there’s no relief. Now he’s home. Spiraling. Now she’s managing that too.
It was nearing the end of my therapy session. I had been rambling for 50 minutes about the mental load, the changing hormones, whether my postpartum depression could really just be traced to the fact that it took longer than anticipated to fit back into my jeans. Then my therapist interrupted and asked what exactly my partner did for work again. “Oh,” I said. “Well, he’s head of AI at his company.”
What she said next, I had to write down. Her client base, she allowed, is almost entirely women—women whose husbands, more often than not, are in some way professionally adjacent to AI. And it’s affecting their relationships. The pressure to keep up means zero boundaries at home. The very masculine energy of it all. And the constant fighting, which is about something bigger than them. He’s off in another world, a world of prompts and benchmarks and epiphanies, while she’s firmly in this one.
The resentment builds quietly. Several of these sad wives, my therapist added, have turned down job opportunities in AI themselves. Not because they weren’t qualified, but because it’s hard to raise kids and disrupt civilization at the same time.
Princess Diana famously said there were three people in her marriage. For the sad wives of AI, the third is a chatbot. I spoke to a few other family therapists, and they agreed with mine: The phenomenon is getting worse. “It’s a lot of tech wives,” one said, sighing. “A lot of tech wives.”
A tiktok meme has been making the rounds recently: young women at their laptops or doing their makeup, captioned something like, “Working so hard so my man can work on his AI startup that loses $30K a month.” The comments section stands in solidarity: “I’m ded.” “Yas queen.” “Just so he can have ‘founder’ in his bio.” I tried to reach out to some of these women. None bit.
I should also say I didn’t bother speaking to any of the actual husbands for this story. I’m sick of hearing from the men of AI. So many of us are. They have podcasts and Senate hearings and magazine profiles and probably a group chat with the president. They’ve been talked to—and I can’t stress this enough—enough.
On an unseasonably warm evening, I met up with two friends at a wine bar. Both are partnered with men somewhere on the AI spectrum—tangibly building it, wildly chasing it, or simply unable to shut up about it. We ordered something orange and natural, the kind of wine that signals you have opinions.
We were in Oakland, which has always prided itself on being the anti–San Francisco—more diversity, less venture-funded cold brew. It has never been home to a single major tech company. It didn’t matter. Within four minutes, we were talking about AI.
It’s so existential. I think about it and then I get depressed.
Yeah. Don’t think about it!
We thought about it for the next two hours.
Every night, it’s just existential dread.
And then, the men. Neither of my friends’ husbands actually makes money from AI. Not yet.
There is this sense, I offered, among people in AI—and people adjacent to it, and people who are pretty sure it’s coming for them—that this is their last chance. They’ve tried everything else, these men, from writing screenplays to investing in crypto. It’s AI or bust. Their partners, meanwhile, have quietly taken on a second job: emotional support. Chief Existential Officer, uncompensated. No one asked us if we wanted the gig.
So what happens now?
Maybe we’ll just go back to the Stone Age.
One friend has started lobbying for her family to become Outdoor People. The kind who go into the wilderness and disconnect. For a whole week, no access. Just don’t tell Claude.
A pause.
Do we want dessert?
Here’s how Bridget Balajadia, a clinician at Lupine Counseling in San Jose, characterizes the AI husband’s situation: “If you don’t respond to an email at midnight, you could wake up and not have a job.” It’s relentless. “In this industry, you’re reachable all the time. You’re thinking about it in the shower, when you’re having sex, it never leaves.” And when it never leaves, the relationship buckles. “It turns into this around-the-clock thing where neither partner is getting what they need. They’re both building walls of resentment.”
Which—we know already. But then Balajadia tells me two surprising things. The first is that some sad wives of AI don’t want to talk to her about their husbands. Why? “I’ve already worked through this with my chat,” they say. By which they mean … ChatGPT. Yes. Not only is AI driving a wedge between couples. It’s also become a primary tool for attempting to salvage their marriage.
Balajadia isn’t impressed. “They’re not having great outcomes,” she says. “It’s not going to challenge you. You end up being validated. Then both of you don’t move the needle in conflict.”
It gets worse. ChatGPT subsequently, in some situations, helps these sad wives explore the possibility of cheating. Some of them, Balajadia says, get “validating messages,” such as: “Yes, it makes sense that you’re seeking attraction elsewhere because your partner’s not giving it to you. He’s emotionally unavailable.” She pauses. “That’s probably not a great idea. You probably should address the stuff that’s coming up in your marriage, not go have sex with someone else.”
Some wives, it must be said, have uncomplicated relationships with AI. One tells me it has “supercharged” her life—wedding planning, caring for aging parents, housekeeping, veterinary advice. While her husband is focused on how AI will change the economy, she’s interested in how it will change her. Optimize her, really. “There’s just not enough hours in the day if I don’t try to gain efficiencies in some things.” In fact, she’s just vibe coded something or other. Maybe one day he’ll be a sad AI husband.
Or robots will fix everything. Another wife tells me that her husband, who founded an AI startup, is convinced they will have a household robot within the decade. “Maybe after we have kids, I’ll be like, ‘Bring a robot in,’” she says. “Right now, I can’t wrap my mind around it, though maybe people felt that way about washing machines.” This in response to the question I ask everyone: Has any part of the AI boom made things better at home? Could it ever?
The responses are generally uninspiring. Most of the time, the closest thing to a silver lining any sad wife can offer is that AI has given them something new to talk about at dinner.
Each time it’s the same pattern: a generation (of men) convinced this is their moment, and everyone else trying to figure out where they fit. A bubble. And bubbles, as anyone who was here in 2001 can tell you, tend to burst. One AI wife—the one who drives past billboards for companies her husband has backed—puts it simply: “Half of our income is dependent on AI doing well.”
Mine too. More than half, to be frank.
Flying home from that same trip to Massachusetts, my husband found himself watching the screen of the passenger next to him. It was playing Train Dreams, a movie about a man who leaves his family for logging and railroad work in the American West, a century ago. Even without sound, he got a little emotional. “Is that what I’m doing right now?” he asked me later.
The man in the film ultimately loses his wife and young daughter. He’s filled with regret for much of his life.
“But I’m doing it for our daughter,” my husband assured me. And: “I’ve always wanted the things I’ve worked on to be necessary.”
I thought about that for a while. Then I asked him to take the dog out.
What Say You?

articles.title: Meet the Sad Wives of AI
articles.body:
If i had to listen to another minute of my husband talking about Claude Code, I might have actually died. It was 11 pm in Berkeley, California, where I was home alone with our 10-month-old daughter, and 2 am in Cambridge, Massachusetts, where he was visiting for his newish job in AI. “JUST LOOK AT THIS!” he shouted. The FaceTime camera zoomed toward a laptop sitting on a hotel bed. “SEE?!”
See what, I thought. I wanted to shower. I still had to take the dog out.
“ARE YOU LOOKING?” he shouted again. I wasn’t. I was looking at our real baby. But that’s the thing. There are two babies in this household now: the small human one and the large language model. Both demand constant attention. Both keep us up at 2 am.
Is this a Sophie’s choice kind of situation? Please. I’d kill the AI baby in an instant.
There’s a strange and under-discussed side effect of the AI boom: what it’s doing to family dynamics. By which I mean: how it’s potentially destroying family dynamics. I’m sure this applies to all kinds of families, gay or straight, rich or poor, with any AI-pilled members. The technology is coming, has come, for us all. But for the purposes of this story, I mostly spoke to white-collar heteros in the Bay Area, because that’s where a certain psychological crisis seems most acute. Often it goes like this: He works in AI, and she does everything and anything else. Other times, it’s bleaker: He desperately wants to work in AI—or feels he must work in AI—and she wants him to do literally anything else.
Either way, the men go in and the women want out. How many? It depends on how you define “working in AI.” About 71 percent of “AI-skilled workers,” according to one report, are men, and there are roughly 35,000 open AI roles in the US at any given moment. Broaden that to include investors and you’re adding thousands more. Broaden it further to include every man who has mentioned to his wife that he is “looking at some opportunities in the space”—and we’re in the millions. Conservatively, that means hundreds of thousands of spouses, partners, and girlfriends, holding down the fort while someone mansplains the singularity to them. There are, in other words, a lot of us, and more of us are surfacing—gasping for air and a single conversation that doesn’t involve LLMs—by the day.
There’s a name for our ranks. I call us the sad wives of AI.
First of all, I’m sorry. AI is already the only thing most people talk about here, and it’s even worse for the sad wives.
One of them moved from New York for her husband’s career. He cofounded an AI company; now he’s head of design at another. “He’s so passionate about it,” she says. “I go along to get along.” That is, when she can remember what it is he does, exactly. “My eyes glaze over a bit. I tend to check out. I forget.” She does say his company is at the forefront of … something. Mostly, she’s tired. “I did not expect how homogenous it would be,” she says. “In New York, I had a friend who’s a teacher, a friend who’s a nurse, a friend in fashion, a friend in finance—and none of us talked about our jobs when we went out. Every time I go out in San Francisco, it feels like I’m at a work happy hour. I don’t get it.”
In a way, it can’t be helped. Most days it feels like every billboard in the city is about AI. Every. Single. One. “I’m on the edge,” another AI wife tells me, “while my husband drives by and is like, ‘Oh wow, that’s my company’s billboard.’ Cool. Great.” She, like almost every sad AI wife I talk to, doesn’t want me to include the specifics of her situation. Marriages, social standings, and finances—anything to protect the equity!—are on the line.
Some of the sad wives are obscenely rich; others are struggling. But the more I talk to them, the more I hear the same lines, the same complaints, the same clichés. The hours. The obsession. The sense that missing this moment would mean, for their AI-pilled spouses, missing the most important technological shift of a lifetime. “They really want to ride the wave,” one AI wife says. Another: “He’s always depressed about something.”
Yana van der Meulen Rodgers, the chair of labor studies and employment relations at Rutgers University, has a blunt take: What’s happening in Bay Area households isn’t just a lifestyle story. It’s a labor market story. The AI boom, Rodgers says, is creating a “perfect storm” of forces reshaping household dynamics, playing out along predictably gendered lines.
The story is older than Silicon Valley, of course. Every major technological boom has produced the same figure, the person who gives everything to the wave. During the industrial revolution, it was the factory worker. During the Gold Rush, it was the men who left their families and headed west. During the dotcom boom, it was the founders sleeping under their desks in SoMa. Now, it is the person who is building, building, always building—vibe coding at midnight, constantly upgrading their models—convinced that stopping for five minutes means missing everything. Economists call this the “ideal worker.” Rodgers calls it a trap. “Someone who works many hours, giving all of themselves to this new force,” she says. “That means less time at home for the partner, less time for care work.”
Though things keep changing, some analyses suggest that women are about 20 percent less likely than men to use generative AI. “It’s a function not of gender per se,” Rodgers suggests, “but of the occupations that women hold.” Women are disproportionately represented in jobs—education, health care, social services—that right now use AI less. The result could be a compounding disadvantage. Over time, it means less access to the boom’s financial rewards, more responsibility for the domestic labor it generates.
And what happens when it doesn’t work out for the men? Many, if not most, won’t make it in AI, a lucrative but volatile business. “With job loss comes some depression,” Rodgers says. “Within the household, if one person is going through adverse mental health effects around job loss or uncertainty, the other naturally becomes the support person.” The cruel irony, for some sad wives, is that the moment their husband does leave AI, whether by choice or by force, there’s no relief. Now he’s home. Spiraling. Now she’s managing that too.
It was nearing the end of my therapy session. I had been rambling for 50 minutes about the mental load, the changing hormones, whether my postpartum depression could really just be traced to the fact that it took longer than anticipated to fit back into my jeans. Then my therapist interrupted and asked what exactly my partner did for work again. “Oh,” I said. “Well, he’s head of AI at his company.”
What she said next, I had to write down. Her client base, she allowed, is almost entirely women—women whose husbands, more often than not, are in some way professionally adjacent to AI. And it’s affecting their relationships. The pressure to keep up means zero boundaries at home. The very masculine energy of it all. And the constant fighting, which is about something bigger than them. He’s off in another world, a world of prompts and benchmarks and epiphanies, while she’s firmly in this one.
The resentment builds quietly. Several of these sad wives, my therapist added, have turned down job opportunities in AI themselves. Not because they weren’t qualified, but because it’s hard to raise kids and disrupt civilization at the same time.
Princess Diana famously said there were three people in her marriage. For the sad wives of AI, the third is a chatbot. I spoke to a few other family therapists, and they agreed with mine: The phenomenon is getting worse. “It’s a lot of tech wives,” one said, sighing. “A lot of tech wives.”
A tiktok meme has been making the rounds recently: young women at their laptops or doing their makeup, captioned something like, “Working so hard so my man can work on his AI startup that loses $30K a month.” The comments section stands in solidarity: “I’m ded.” “Yas queen.” “Just so he can have ‘founder’ in his bio.” I tried to reach out to some of these women. None bit.
I should also say I didn’t bother speaking to any of the actual husbands for this story. I’m sick of hearing from the men of AI. So many of us are. They have podcasts and Senate hearings and magazine profiles and probably a group chat with the president. They’ve been talked to—and I can’t stress this enough—enough.
On an unseasonably warm evening, I met up with two friends at a wine bar. Both are partnered with men somewhere on the AI spectrum—tangibly building it, wildly chasing it, or simply unable to shut up about it. We ordered something orange and natural, the kind of wine that signals you have opinions.
We were in Oakland, which has always prided itself on being the anti–San Francisco—more diversity, less venture-funded cold brew. It has never been home to a single major tech company. It didn’t matter. Within four minutes, we were talking about AI.
It’s so existential. I think about it and then I get depressed.
Yeah. Don’t think about it!
We thought about it for the next two hours.
Every night, it’s just existential dread.
And then, the men. Neither of my friends’ husbands actually makes money from AI. Not yet.
There is this sense, I offered, among people in AI—and people adjacent to it, and people who are pretty sure it’s coming for them—that this is their last chance. They’ve tried everything else, these men, from writing screenplays to investing in crypto. It’s AI or bust. Their partners, meanwhile, have quietly taken on a second job: emotional support. Chief Existential Officer, uncompensated. No one asked us if we wanted the gig.
So what happens now?
Maybe we’ll just go back to the Stone Age.
One friend has started lobbying for her family to become Outdoor People. The kind who go into the wilderness and disconnect. For a whole week, no access. Just don’t tell Claude.
A pause.
Do we want dessert?
Here’s how Bridget Balajadia, a clinician at Lupine Counseling in San Jose, characterizes the AI husband’s situation: “If you don’t respond to an email at midnight, you could wake up and not have a job.” It’s relentless. “In this industry, you’re reachable all the time. You’re thinking about it in the shower, when you’re having sex, it never leaves.” And when it never leaves, the relationship buckles. “It turns into this around-the-clock thing where neither partner is getting what they need. They’re both building walls of resentment.”
Which—we know already. But then Balajadia tells me two surprising things. The first is that some sad wives of AI don’t want to talk to her about their husbands. Why? “I’ve already worked through this with my chat,” they say. By which they mean … ChatGPT. Yes. Not only is AI driving a wedge between couples. It’s also become a primary tool for attempting to salvage their marriage.
Balajadia isn’t impressed. “They’re not having great outcomes,” she says. “It’s not going to challenge you. You end up being validated. Then both of you don’t move the needle in conflict.”
It gets worse. ChatGPT subsequently, in some situations, helps these sad wives explore the possibility of cheating. Some of them, Balajadia says, get “validating messages,” such as: “Yes, it makes sense that you’re seeking attraction elsewhere because your partner’s not giving it to you. He’s emotionally unavailable.” She pauses. “That’s probably not a great idea. You probably should address the stuff that’s coming up in your marriage, not go have sex with someone else.”
Some wives, it must be said, have uncomplicated relationships with AI. One tells me it has “supercharged” her life—wedding planning, caring for aging parents, housekeeping, veterinary advice.
